name: Fake tooth caps / press-on veneers

card.summary: DIY removable covers for the teeth; no studies on them exist.
card.note: No published research on these over-the-counter products.

quick.overview:
These are removable cosmetic shells placed over the front teeth to change how they look. They are not the same as dentist-made bonded veneers.

No published studies on the retail products were found.
quick.mechanism: The shell sits over the natural teeth, usually without bonding or tooth preparation.
quick.risks: Safety and fit have not been studied in published research; professional veneer literature does not cover these products.

lead: Press-on veneers and fake tooth caps, also sold as snap-on or clip-on veneers, are removable cosmetic covers placed over the front of the teeth to change their apparent shape, length or shade. People use them to hide chips, gaps, stains or missing teeth for a more even, brighter smile without dental drilling, and some wear them for photos or events.[1][2][3]

They differ from dental veneers, which are thin layers of composite or porcelain bonded to the tooth by a dentist.[1] Colgate describes snap-on veneers as sitting over the teeth like a mouthguard and being removable by the wearer, with professionally made versions produced from molds of the teeth sent to a lab and checked at a fitting.[3] A dentistry-news summary notes that, unlike porcelain veneers, they do not require enamel adjustment.[2]

Dental organisations and clinicians have raised concerns about over-the-counter versions. An American Dental Association news item summarising expert commentary says plastic snap-on veneers can trap food against the teeth, raising the risk of decay and gum disease, and can damage enamel.[2] No published trial of their fit, safety or longevity was found.

chain: A thin plastic or resin shell is placed over the front teeth

angle.text: The cover changes how the teeth look while it is worn, hiding discolouration, small gaps and uneven edges. It is removable, so the look is temporary and no enamel is removed.

paras: Dental veneers were invented by California dentist Charles Pincus in 1928 as a temporary way to alter actors' teeth on film sets, and in 1937 he made acrylic versions held by denture adhesive, which bonded poorly.[1] Michael Buonocore introduced acid etching in 1959, and Simonsen and Calamia's 1982 finding that porcelain could be etched enabled strong bonds and permanent porcelain veneers.[1]

Removable covers are marketed as a less permanent alternative to traditional veneers for people who are not ready for permanent work or want to try a look first.[3] They can cover missing or gapped teeth and yellowed or stained teeth, but do not change tooth structure and cannot fix severe crooked teeth, which Colgate says an orthodontist should address.[3] Social media coverage popularised cheaper plastic versions that cover missing, discoloured or chipped teeth.[2]

Wikipedia reports that composite veneers last about four years, that an inexperienced dentist may remove 3 to 30 percent of the tooth surface during preparation for porcelain veneers, and that about half of veneers need re-treatment or replacement after ten years, though it flags some figures for verification.[1] Press-on covers are marketed as avoiding tooth preparation.[2][3]

The ADA News item reports experts warning that plastic snap-on veneers can trap food particles and raise the risk of tooth decay and gum disease, do not match the quality of porcelain veneers and can damage enamel.[2] Colgate states that no type of veneer can replace good dental healthcare.[3]
No studies found of over-the-counter press-on or snap-on veneers.
